source.basis: Operator spec page; structured facts only, no operator prose reproduced.

reading.body:
CyrusOne's Lebanon, Ohio campus publishes 35 MW of IT capacity, the largest published figure of any mapped Ohio data center, in a state where only 9 of 79 mapped facilities publish a megawatt figure at all.

That gap is the real finding. The 9 published Ohio facilities sum to 118.4 MW, so this single campus is close to 30 percent of the state's known total. Ohio's data center footprint is largely invisible at the level of power, which means one campus with a published number anchors the entire state's known capacity. For AI specifically, published power is the scarce input, not floor space, and this campus is one of the few places in Ohio where the power number is on the record.

The 35 MW is a power figure, not a rack count. The operator publishes no rack count and no per-rack density, so any conversion to accelerators depends on an assumption the data does not supply. At 40 kW per rack, a common density for AI training halls, 35 MW is roughly 875 racks, but that is arithmetic on an assumed density, not a claim by CyrusOne. The 400,000 square feet of technical space establishes room for a substantial compute footprint, and nothing in the data establishes which accelerators, if any, are deployed there.

The certifications, SOC 2 Type 2, PCI DSS, HIPAA, ISO 27001, FISMA, SSAE 16 Type II, and Green Globes, qualify the campus for specific classes of regulated work. None names a tenant. The spec page publishes no tenants, no pricing, and no interconnection details. Whether AI workloads actually run at Lebanon is not published, and the data does not answer it.

suitability.basis: weighted mean of the published inputs named here, scaled to 100; formula on the methodology page
